messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Counselor
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 43

She is 32, a South Asian woman who now works as a school counselor, and when she tells her story it tends to begin in fragments: the metallic rattle of shutters being pulled down too fast, the sudden silence after a blast, her mother pushing her and her younger brother into a hallway away from the windows. She grew up in a city that gradually became a war zone, the ordinary rhythms of family life narrowing around checkpoints, shelling, and rumor. At first she remembers insisting on normalcy. She studies for exams by candlelight during power cuts, walks to school with her books clutched to her chest, and learns to judge distance by sound—whether gunfire is near enough to run from or far enough to ignore.

The event she returns to most often happens in her early twenties, before she leaves the country. That morning begins like many others, with negotiation over whether it is safe enough to go out. Her father needs medicine for his blood pressure, and she goes with him because she is the one in the family who speaks firmly and calmly at checkpoints. On the way back, the street erupts. There is shouting first, then the crack of gunfire, then an explosion so forceful it seems to lift the air out of her lungs. She remembers being on the ground without remembering how she got there. Dust fills her mouth. A car burns nearby. Her father is a few feet away, bleeding and stunned, and she cannot hear him although his lips are moving. She tries to drag him behind a concrete barrier while people run in every direction. A second blast comes somewhere close enough that she feels it in her ribs. For a few seconds she is sure they are both about to die.

Her father survives the attack but never fully recovers physically. What stays with her even more than the images is the feeling that the world can split open without warning. After that day, she starts scanning every street before stepping into it. She sits near exits. She startles when a door slams and feels humiliated by how visibly she jumps. At night she lies awake, replaying the sequence with compulsive precision: if they had left ten minutes later, if she had chosen another pharmacy, if she had pulled him faster. Sleep, when it comes, is thin and punishing. She wakes with her heart racing after dreams in which she is trying to speak but no sound comes out, or she is running through smoke carrying something precious she cannot see.

When she emigrates several years later after marrying, her relatives describe it as a new beginning. On the surface, she agrees. She is bright, warm, and composed, and in her new country she builds a respectable life. She trains and then works as a school counselor, a role that fits the part of her that has always been able to remain steady for other people. She is excellent with distressed children. She notices the quiet one in the corner, the child who flinches at raised voices, the teenager who says “I’m fine” too quickly. Colleagues admire her patience.

What they do not see is what it costs her. Fire drills are the worst. The alarm slices through her body before her mind catches up, and for an instant she is no longer in a school corridor but back in that street, lungs clenched, eyes searching for debris and blood. She keeps her face arranged for the children, guiding them outside in an even voice, while sweat collects under her collar and her hands tremble around the attendance clipboard. Afterwards she often needs to sit alone in her office with the lights dimmed, ashamed that a routine safety exercise can unravel her.

At home, her husband knows more of the private terrain. He sees how she checks the locks twice before bed and how she prefers the television volume low because sudden loud sounds make her chest tighten. He has learned not to come up behind her in the kitchen. Some nights she wakes gasping and pushes herself upright before she fully knows where she is. On those nights she walks through the apartment, looking out the windows, as though vigilance itself could keep disaster away. She feels guilty for the distance this creates. She wants softness and ease in her marriage, but she often feels watchful instead, as if tenderness requires a surrender she cannot safely make.

She also avoids more than she first admits. She does not go to crowded festivals, cannot tolerate news footage of bombed buildings, and has stopped attending large community gatherings after once freezing at the sound of fireworks, her mind instantly furnishing screams and smoke. She tells people she is busy. Part of her fears that if she lets herself fully remember, she will be swallowed by it; another part resents that memory intrudes anyway, in smells, in sirens, in the sight of a father holding a daughter’s hand on the sidewalk.

What troubles her most in the present is the split between her outer competence and inner exhaustion. She is the person others rely on in moments of upset, yet she moves through many days braced for catastrophe. She wants to be present with the students she counsels, with her husband, with the life she has built. Instead she often feels as though one part of her is still crouched behind that concrete barrier, listening for the next blast, waiting for proof that the danger has truly passed.
